title: Revisiting the Optical F-corona from the Artemis II Total Solar Eclipse with RAW Data: How Far Can Consumer JPEG Images Be Trusted for Astronomical Photometry?

paper.title: Revisiting the Optical F-corona from the Artemis II Total Solar Eclipse with RAW Data: How Far Can Consumer JPEG Images Be Trusted for Astronomical Photometry?
paper.abstract: Abstract We reanalyze the total solar eclipse images taken with a consumer camera during the Artemis II lunar flyby, using the RAW data as ground truth for our previous analysis of the released JPEG image. Calibrated with field stars, the RAW data show that the lens vignetting and the variation of the pixel solid angle reduce the signal of diffuse light by up to ∼ \sim 70% at the edge of the field, and that the signal on the dark side of the Moon is most likely foreground light rather than an instrumental offset. Between 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} and 15 ∘ 15^{\circ} elongation, the radial profiles of the F-corona follow power laws with indices of − 2.0 -2.0 to − 2.3 -2.3 (east), − 2.5 -2.5 (west), and − 2.4 -2.4 to − 2.7 -2.7 (north and south), consistent with space-based observations, and the surface brightness along the ecliptic is ∼ \sim 26 MJy sr -1 ( ± 7 % \pm 7\% ) at 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} . The isophotes have flattening indices of ∼ \sim 0.6–0.7 and superellipse indices of ∼ \sim 1.5–1.6. Comparison with the ZodiSURF zodiacal light model supports a radial dust density index of α ≃ 1.3 \alpha\simeq 1.3 down to ∼ \sim 0.2 au and suggests that the vertical distribution of the dust broadens toward the Sun. The JPEG image retains nearly the full vignetting, despite its metadata, and its tone response is not a single power law; together with the zero-point treatment, these effects account for the steep and asymmetric profiles reported previously, while the flattened morphology and α ≃ 1.3 \alpha\simeq 1.3 are confirmed. We identify quantities robust in JPEG images and show that the tone response can be reconstructed from field stars.

sections.heading: I.1 The F-corona and the Moon as a natural occulter
sections.text: The Fraunhofer corona (F-corona) is the inner extension of the zodiacal light, produced by sunlight scattered by interplanetary dust particles close to the Sun [ 52 , 32 ] . Its brightness distribution traces the structure of the inner zodiacal cloud. Because the F-corona must be observed against the photospheric glare, observations have relied on coronagraphs and heliospheric imagers, such as LASCO on board SOHO [ 28 ] , the Heliospheric Imager on board STEREO [ 44 ] , and WISPR on board the Parker Solar Probe [ 43 ] , or on eclipse-like geometries in which a planetary body blocks the solar disk [ 17 ] . The use of the lunar disk as a natural, low-stray-light occulter dates back to the Surveyor missions [ 36 , 7 ] and has been revisited as a concept for routine coronal observations from lunar orbit [ 16 , 12 ] . The Artemis II crewed lunar flyby provided such a geometry. On 2026 April 7, about two hours after closest approach, the crew photographed the totally eclipsed Sun from the Orion spacecraft with a handheld consumer digital camera, and NASA released the image art002e009301 as an 8-bit RGB JPEG image on the same day. Using this image, Tsumura and Arimatsu [50, hereafter TA26] investigated the large-scale morphology of the optical F-corona over solar elongations of ∼ \sim 7 ∘ –38 ∘ . They reported a flattened distribution aligned with the ecliptic (flattening indices f = 0.52 f=0.52 – 0.56 0.56 ; Equation 5 in Section IV.3 ), radial profiles that are systematically steeper than those derived from STEREO/HI-1A [ 44 ] , and a radial dust density index of α ∼ 1.3 \alpha\sim 1.3 from a comparison with the ZodiSURF model [ 38 ] .

sections.heading: I.2 Consumer-camera JPEG images as astronomical data
sections.text: Images taken with consumer digital cameras are increasingly used for scientific purposes, including measurements of night-sky brightness and artificial light at night [ 18 , 41 ] , photometry of bright stars [ 11 ] , and morphological studies in which absolute calibration is not required [ 34 , 27 ] . Rendered products such as JPEG images are often the only form in which an observation is made public, especially for opportunistic observations from crewed spacecraft. A JPEG image, however, is a rendering of the incident flux rather than a measurement of it: the processing chain typically includes demosaicing, white balancing, a color-space transformation that mixes the camera channels, a tone curve, optional lens corrections, quantization to 8 bits, and lossy compression, most of which are camera- and software-specific and poorly documented [ 9 , e.g.,] . Any analysis of a JPEG image must therefore assume a model for the inverse of this chain, which usually cannot be verified from the JPEG image itself. TA26 defined the zero point of each channel by the signal on the dark side of the lunar disk, modeled the tone response as a single power law, S ∝ F Γ S\propto F^{\Gamma} , between the JPEG signal S S and the incident flux F F , with Γ = 0.700 \Gamma=0.700 , 0.725, and 0.825 for the red, green, and blue channels calibrated with field stars, and assumed that vignetting had been removed by the processing, as indicated by the image metadata. Each of these steps was reasonable given the available data, but none of them could be tested independently.

sections.heading: I.3 This work: RAW data as ground truth
sections.text: On 2026 October 7, the original camera RAW files of the Artemis II lunar flyby images were archived in the NASA Planetary Data System [ 4 ] . For art002e009301 , this provides the 14-bit sensor data of exactly the same exposure that was analyzed in TA26. Such a pairing of a rendered JPEG image and the corresponding RAW data for a scientifically analyzed astronomical target offers a rare opportunity to check every assumption of a JPEG-based analysis quantitatively. The purpose of this paper is twofold. First, we re-derive the properties of the F-corona from the RAW data with a full reduction, including an in situ flat-field correction, a characterization of the zero point, and an absolute calibration. A second frame with a three times longer exposure ( art002e009300 ), reduced independently, provides a key check that the results do not depend on a single image. Second, we use the RAW data to evaluate how each step of the JPEG-based analysis affected the results of TA26, and we assess which quantities can and cannot be derived reliably from consumer-camera JPEG images. Throughout this paper, “ground truth” refers to the closest available representation of the sensor measurements: the RAW data are themselves stored with a non-reversible compression (Section II.2 ) and are therefore not strictly identical to the original sensor output. Section II describes the data, Section III the reduction of the RAW data, and Section IV the properties of the F-corona derived from them. Section V compares the RAW and JPEG analyses, Section VI discusses the capabilities and limitations of JPEG-based analysis, and Section VII summarizes this work.

sections.heading: II.2 RAW data
sections.text: We used the original camera files in Nikon Electronic Format (NEF) from the Artemis II Crew Camera Bundle of the NASA Planetary Data System [ 4 ] , rather than the processed products of the bundle [ 5 ] , so that the entire reduction could be controlled. The NEF files are recorded with the “High efficiency ⋆ \star ” (HE ∗ ) option of the camera, a non-reversible compression based on the TicoRAW codec [ 24 ] , which, according to the manufacturer, produces pictures that compare favorably in quality to those recorded with lossless compression [ 35 ] . We converted the NEF files into the Digital Negative (DNG) format with Adobe DNG Converter [ 2 , version 18.7;] , which decodes the HE ∗ data without further processing, and read the DNG files with rawpy [ 40 ] . The conversion preserves the undemosaiced sensor data; possible effects of the HE ∗ compression on faint signals could not be evaluated directly, but the linear response of the stellar signals (Section III.6 ) and the agreement of all results between the two frames, whose signal levels differ by a factor of three, show no evidence of them. We use the full sensor area (Table 1 ); the default crop of the DNG files starts at pixel ( x , y ) = ( 12 , 8 ) (x,y)=(12,8) and matches the size of the released JPEG image.

sections.heading: II.3 JPEG image
sections.text: For the comparison with TA26, we used the JPEG version of art002e009301 released by NASA. According to its metadata, it was rendered from the RAW file with Adobe Photoshop Lightroom Classic about four hours after the exposure, using the Adobe lens profile for the lens and camera with both distortion and vignetting corrections flagged as applied. The coefficients of the radial distortion model are recorded, and the full lens profile, including a vignetting model, is also embedded in the DNG files. The parameters of the other rendering steps (tone curve, color rendering, and any local adjustments) are not recorded. The actual processing is evaluated in Section V.1 .

Because of the wide field and the strong distortion, Simple Imaging Polynomial [ 42 , SIP;] distortion terms of order 3 or 4 leave residuals of ∼ \sim 45 ′′ , and we adopted a gnomonic (TAN) projection [ 10 ] with sixth-order SIP terms. sections.text: Because no flat-field frame is available, the vignetting was determined in situ from aperture photometry of the BSC5 stars (radius of 32 pixels, local background in an annulus of 40–50 pixels, saturated stars excluded). The difference between the instrumental and catalog magnitudes was modeled with an even-order polynomial in ρ \rho , a form commonly used for the radial light falloff of camera lenses [ 15 , 1 , e.g.,] : m inst − V = z k + c ⁡ ( B − V ) + a 2 ​ ρ 2 + a 4 ​ ρ 4 , m_{\rm inst}-V=z_{k}+c\,(B-V)+a_{2}\rho^{2}+a_{4}\rho^{4}, (1) where z k z_{k} is a zero point for frame k k and c c is a color coefficient. Fitting the two frames jointly (420–430 stars per channel) gives the relative throughput T ⁡ ( ρ ) = 10 − 0.4 ​ ( a 2 ​ ρ 2 + a 4 ​ ρ 4 ) T(\rho)=10^{-0.4\,(a_{2}\rho^{2}+a_{4}\rho^{4})} (2) shown in Figure 2 (a) and (c). The light loss in the green channel is 0.25 ± 0.02 0.25\pm 0.02 , 0.57 ± 0.03 0.57\pm 0.03 , and 0.92 ± 0.02 0.92\pm 0.02 mag at ρ = 0.5 \rho=0.5 , 0.75, and 0.94, respectively, and is larger in the blue and smaller in the red channel by ≲ \lesssim 0.12 mag. Strong vignetting of this lens at full aperture is also reported in a published lens review, which found a light loss of 46% in the image corners on a full-frame sensor [ 37 ] ; the exact position of that measurement is not documented, but the value is comparable to that of our model for a uniformly illuminated target (green channel, including the pixel solid angle), 48%–53% at ρ = 0.7 \rho=0.7 –0.75. The main systematic uncertainty is the dependence on the aperture: the point-spread function broadens toward the field edges, so that apertures smaller than 32 pixels overestimate the vignetting, while apertures of 32 and 48 pixels agree within 0.05 mag at ρ ≤ 0.75 \rho\leq 0.75 and ∼ \sim 0.1 mag at ρ = 0.94 \rho=0.94 . Freeing the position of the optical axis (consistent with the image center within ∼ \sim 50 pixels), adding a ρ 6 \rho^{6} term, or fitting the frames separately changes the flat field by ≲ \lesssim 0.04–0.08 mag. A fit with the synthetic RGB magnitudes of Cardiel et al. [11] , the catalog used in TA26, agrees within 1–2 σ \sigma ; it requires no color term but includes only ∼ \sim 45 stars. The calibration stars extend to ρ = 0.94 \rho=0.94 ; the model is extrapolated only in the corners of the field, which affect only the outermost profile bins, not used quantitatively. For diffuse emission, the signal per pixel is in addition proportional to Ω \Omega , and the surface brightness is I ⁡ ( x , y ) ∝ F ⁡ ( x , y ) T ⁡ ( ρ ) ​ Ω ​ ( x , y ) / Ω 0 − I Z , I(x,y)\propto\frac{F(x,y)}{T(\rho)\,\Omega(x,y)/\Omega_{0}}-I_{Z}, (3) where F F is the signal in the linear image and I Z I_{Z} is the zero point (Section III.5 ).

sections.heading: III.5 Zero Point and Stray Light
sections.text: Following TA26, we use the dark side of the lunar disk to determine the zero point. The dark-side region is the part of the disk within 0.8 ​ R M 0.8\,R_{\rm M} of its center, more than 0.2 ​ R M 0.2\,R_{\rm M} from it toward + x +x , and less than 0.3 ​ R M 0.3\,R_{\rm M} from it toward + y +y ( R M R_{\rm M} is the lunar radius), which avoids the limb, the earthshine-illuminated eastern part, and a faint brighter band near the southern limb (Figure 1 (c)). In art002e009301 , the mean signals in this region are 19, 46, and 50 ADU in the red, green, and blue channels. This signal is not mainly an instrumental offset: from art002e009301 to art002e009300 , it increases by factors of 3.1–3.3, close to the ratio of the effective exposure times measured from stars (2.95–3.12). It shows no lunar surface features, which disfavors illumination of the night side of the Moon, and it is bluer than the F-corona, which disfavors F-corona light scattered within the camera or by the window. After scaling by the exposure-time ratio, its spatial distribution agrees between the two frames at the same detector position (rms difference of 2.9 ADU in the green channel) but not when the frames are aligned on the star field (6.8 ADU), which excludes sources fixed on the sky. Because the Moon was almost fixed on the detector, however, light fixed to the camera and light associated with the Moon cannot be distinguished in this way. Figure 3: Stellar signals in the RAW data of art002e009301 as a function of catalog magnitude for the red, green, and blue channels (left to right). Top: V V magnitudes of BSC5. Bottom: synthetic RGB magnitudes of Cardiel et al. [11] . Black symbols show the unsaturated stars fainter than 4 mag used in the fits, gray symbols the unsaturated brighter stars, and red open circles the stars with saturated RAW pixels. The signals are measured within a radius of 16 pixels after local background subtraction and corrected with the flat field. Solid lines show the linear fits, with the slopes and the numbers of stars given in each panel, and dashed lines show the slope of − 0.4 -0.4 expected for a linear response. A further constraint is provided by the darkest parts of the sky. If the dark-side signal were uniform on the detector, every sky pixel would exceed it; instead, the mean signals in the northwestern corner of the field are lower than the dark-side signal by 5–26 ADU, i.e., by more than 100 times their uncertainties, so that 3%–13% of the sky becomes negative when the dark-side signal is subtracted uniformly from the image signal. The same comparison in surface brightness, i.e., after division by T ​ Ω / Ω 0 T\,\Omega/\Omega_{0} , shows no sky significantly fainter than the dark side (the faintest sky is 0.97–1.27 times as bright). These observations exclude a detector offset as the main component. Light confined to the lunar disk, already disfavored above, would also make the near equality of the faintest sky and the dark side in surface brightness a coincidence. The observations are naturally explained, although not uniquely, if the dark-side signal is light that enters through the lens and is uniform across the field of view, such as light scattered in front of the camera (e.g., by the spacecraft window), which is subject to the same vignetting and pixel solid angle as the sky. We adopt this interpretation and subtract the mean dark-side surface brightness, I Z = ⟨ F T ​ Ω / Ω 0 ⟩ dark , I_{Z}=\left\langle\frac{F}{T\,\Omega/\Omega_{0}}\right\rangle_{\rm dark}, (4) uniformly in surface brightness (Equation 3 ). As its systematic uncertainty, we adopt half the range of I Z I_{Z} derived from halves of the dark-side region (2%–4%). The two-frame comparison also allows for a constant offset of − 2 -2 to − 6 -6 ADU; subtracting it separately before the flat-field correction changes the power-law indices of Section IV.1 by ≤ 0.07 \leq 0.07 . For reference, if the dark-side signal were instead uniform on the detector (subtracted before the flat-field correction), the indices would be steeper by ≤ 0.2 \leq 0.2 except toward the south (0.3–0.8), and subtracting only the black level ( I Z = 0 I_{Z}=0 ) would make them shallower by up to 0.2 along the ecliptic and 0.6 in the north–south direction.

sections.heading: III.7 Absolute Calibration
sections.text: Because the RAW data are linear, the surface brightness can also be calibrated in absolute units, which was not possible in TA26. We evaluated the zero point of Equation ( 1 ) for the color of the Sun ( B − V = 0.65 B-V=0.65 ), adopted 3636 Jy for V = 0 V=0 [ 6 ] , and applied an aperture correction of 7 % ± 4 % 7\%\pm 4\% for the stellar light outside the 32-pixel aperture, derived from the growth of the signals of bright stars between 16, 32, and 48 pixels. One output unit of the linear image, corrected with Equation ( 3 ), then corresponds to 4.23 × 10 − 3 4.23\times 10^{-3} MJy sr -1 in the green channel, which is closest to the V V band and to which we refer below. A calibration based on 48-pixel apertures gives values lower by ∼ \sim 10%, because the signals of faint stars in larger apertures are affected by errors in the subtraction of the bright, structured background; with stars brighter than V = 5 V=5 only, the two apertures agree within 5%, and the values are 4%–6% higher than nominal. The resulting error budget is summarized in Table 2 ; assuming the components to be independent, the total uncertainty is ± 7 % \pm 7\% . The red and blue channels give values 4%–12% lower, which we regard as a further indication of the systematic uncertainty rather than a color of the F-corona. The zero point I Z I_{Z} corresponds to ∼ \sim 0.9 MJy sr -1 .

sections.heading: IV.2 Color Dependence
sections.text: Toward the west and south, the indices of the three channels agree within 0.12. Toward the east, the profiles become shallower from the red to the blue channel, by + 0.29 ± 0.09 +0.29\pm 0.09 and + 0.25 ± 0.08 +0.25\pm 0.08 (blue minus red) in the two frames, and a similar but less significant trend is seen toward the north. The eastern color difference is reproduced in both frames, is present without the flat-field correction, and is insensitive to the zero point. Systematic effects fixed to the detector, such as a non-radial component of the vignetting that differs between the channels, would however affect both frames in the same way, and we regard this color dependence as tentative. It cannot be explained by contamination from the K-corona: the K-corona has the color of the solar spectrum, whereas the zodiacal light is redder than the solar spectrum from optical to near-infrared wavelengths [ 32 , 49 , e.g.,] , and the K-corona decreases more steeply with elongation than the F-corona [ 53 , 20 ] ; its contamination would thus steepen the profiles in the blue channel rather than flatten them. sections.heading: IV.3 Flattening of the Isophotes
sections.text: The flattening of the F-corona was quantified with the flattening index [ 26 , 44 ] f = R eq R pol − 1 , f=\frac{R_{\rm eq}}{R_{\rm pol}}-1, (5) where R eq R_{\rm eq} and R pol R_{\rm pol} are the equatorial and polar semi-axes of an isophote. From the elongations at which the four profiles reach a given level, the isophotes with R pol ≃ 12 ∘ R_{\rm pol}\simeq 12^{\circ} have f W = R W / R pol − 1 = 0.57 f_{\rm W}=R_{\rm W}/R_{\rm pol}-1=0.57 –0.60 in all channels and both frames, where the western semi-axis R W R_{\rm W} is used because the eastern one reaches the edge of the field. f W f_{\rm W} increases outward (0.64–0.77 and 0.78–0.92 for R pol = 14 ∘ R_{\rm pol}=14^{\circ} and 16 ∘ 16^{\circ} ) and is insensitive to the zero point. Stenborg et al. [44] showed that the isophotes of the F-corona between 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} and 24 ∘ 24^{\circ} are better described by superellipses than by ellipses. Following their Equation (4), a superellipse with center ( x 0 , y 0 ) (x_{0},y_{0}) , semimajor and semiminor axes a a and b b , and tilt ψ \psi is | x ′ a | n + | y ′ b | n = 1 , \left|\frac{x^{\prime}}{a}\right|^{n}+\left|\frac{y^{\prime}}{b}\right|^{n}=1, (6) where x ′ = ( x − x 0 ) ​ cos ⁡ ψ + ( y − y 0 ) ​ sin ⁡ ψ x^{\prime}=(x-x_{0})\cos\psi+(y-y_{0})\sin\psi and y ′ = − ( x − x 0 ) ​ sin ⁡ ψ + ( y − y 0 ) ​ cos ⁡ ψ y^{\prime}=-(x-x_{0})\sin\psi+(y-y_{0})\cos\psi are coordinates along the major and minor axes, and the superellipse index n n defines the shape: n = 2 n=2 gives an ellipse and n < 2 n<2 a more diamond-like curve; the flattening index of Equation ( 5 ) is then f = a / b − 1 f=a/b-1 . Stenborg et al. [44] found n n increasing from ∼ \sim 1.54 to ∼ \sim 1.65 as f f decreases from ∼ \sim 0.66 to ∼ \sim 0.46 toward the Sun. We extracted isophotes from star-removed surface-brightness images projected onto a Sun-centered gnomonic grid and fitted Equation ( 6 ) with all six parameters free (Figure 5 ). Reliable fits are obtained only for isophotes with a ≃ 17 ∘ a\simeq 17^{\circ} – 22 ∘ 22^{\circ} in the red and green channels, for which we obtain n = 1.49 n=1.49 –1.62 and f = 0.57 f=0.57 –0.71, consistent between the two frames within 0.03. The isophotes are thus more diamond-like than ellipses ( n = 2 n=2 ), and the red-channel values lie within ∼ \sim 0.05 of the relation of Stenborg et al. [44] . When the centers are fixed at the Sun, the fits are poorer and n n scatters between 1.4 and 2.1 among the isophotes, because the offsets of the isophote centers (see below) are then absorbed by the shape. We therefore adopt the fits with free centers and use n = 1.55 ± 0.07 n=1.55\pm 0.07 , where the uncertainty represents the range among the frames, channels, and isophotes, as the observed value (Section IV.6.3 ). The fitted centers are offset from the Sun by + 0 ​ . ∘ ​ 4 +0\fdg 4 to + 0 ​ . ∘ ​ 55 +0\fdg 55 toward the north and by up to 1 ​ . ∘ ​ 2 1\fdg 2 toward the east, the latter reflecting the shallower eastern profiles. The northward offset is consistent with the viewing geometry discussed by Stenborg et al. [44] , based on the orientation of the symmetry surface of the dust cloud [ 45 ] : for an observer between its ascending ( ∼ \sim 82 ∘ ) and descending ( ∼ \sim 262 ∘ ) nodes in heliocentric longitude, as in our case ( ∼ \sim 197 ∘ ), the northern part of the cloud is closer and appears brighter.

sections.heading: IV.4 K-corona Contamination
sections.text: The analyzed elongations ( ϵ > 7 ∘ \epsilon>7^{\circ} , i.e., ≳ \gtrsim 25 R ⊙ R_{\odot} ) are beyond the distance of ∼ \sim 4–6 R ⊙ R_{\odot} at which the K- and F-coronae become comparable [ 53 , 20 ] , so that the K-corona is expected to be negligible. As a further test, TA26 compared the profiles along two coronal streamers seen in a publicly available LASCO C3 [ 8 ] image taken 12 minutes before art002e009301 with those along the opposite directions. We repeated this comparison with the same LASCO C3 image and the same sectors as TA26 (Figure 6 ). The ratio of the “on” to “off” profiles is close to unity at the smallest elongations and departs from it outward, decreasing to 0.45–0.75 for S1 and increasing to 1.2–1.9 for S2 at ∼ \sim 20 ∘ , consistently in the two frames. A K-coronal contribution would instead produce an excess along the streamers that is largest near the Sun. The departures follow the large-scale asymmetries found above: the S2 sectors coincide with the eastern and western profiles, and the S1 “off” sector lies in the northeastern quadrant, toward which the isophotes are displaced. We therefore find no evidence for a K-coronal contribution, in agreement with TA26, but unlike TA26, we find a dimming along the streamer only for S1 (see Section V.2 ). sections.heading: IV.5 Absolute Surface Brightness
sections.text: The surface brightness along the ecliptic is ∼ \sim 26 MJy sr -1 at 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} and 9.5–10.6 MJy sr -1 at 15 ∘ 15^{\circ} , and that toward the north and south is 5.2 and 4.2 MJy sr -1 at 12 . ∘ \fdg 5 (Figure 7 ). For comparison, the power-law fits of Stenborg et al. [44] to the eastern photometric axis of the F-corona from STEREO/HI-1A, in units of the mean solar brightness, give I ≃ 10 2.39 ​ ϵ − 2.33 × 10 − 11 ​ B ⊙ I\simeq 10^{2.39}\,\epsilon^{-2.33}\times 10^{-11}\,B_{\odot} ( ϵ \epsilon in degrees) for observers between the nodes of the dust cloud, as in our case. With B ⊙ = 2.66 × 10 12 B_{\odot}=2.66\times 10^{12} MJy sr -1 in the V V band ( V ⊙ = − 26.74 V_{\odot}=-26.74 ), this corresponds to 30.5 and 11.9 MJy sr -1 at 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} and 15 ∘ 15^{\circ} , i.e., 12%–25% brighter than our values, which is consistent given our calibration uncertainty, the different passband of HI-1, and the different observing geometry.

sections.heading: IV.6.1 Model
sections.text: Following TA26, we compared the observations with the zodiacal light model ZodiSURF [ 38 ] , which combines the dust distribution of Kelsall et al. [25] with a scattering phase function and albedo calibrated with HST sky surface-brightness measurements. The density of the smooth cloud is n d ​ ( r , ζ ) = n d , 0 ​ ( r r 0 ) − α ​ exp ⁡ ( − η ​ g γ ) , n_{\rm d}(r,\zeta)=n_{\rm d,0}\left(\frac{r}{r_{0}}\right)^{-\alpha}\exp(-\eta\,g^{\gamma}), (7) with g = { ζ 2 / 2 ​ μ ( ζ < μ ) ζ − μ / 2 ( ζ ≥ μ ) , g=\begin{cases}\zeta^{2}/2\mu&(\zeta<\mu)\\ \zeta-\mu/2&(\zeta\geq\mu)\end{cases}, (8) where r r is the heliocentric distance, n d , 0 n_{\rm d,0} is the density at r 0 = 1 r_{0}=1 au, ζ \zeta is the sine of the latitude above the symmetry plane, and the standard parameters are α = 1.34 \alpha=1.34 , η = 4.14 \eta=4.14 , γ = 0.942 \gamma=0.942 , and μ = 0.189 \mu=0.189 [ 25 ] . We calculated the model surface brightness at wavelengths of 0.60, 0.53, and 0.47 μ \mu m for the three channels (0.55 μ \mu m for the comparison of absolute surface brightness), for an observer at the Earth at the time of the observation, with the model profiles computed relative to the solar position used internally by the model. Because the model is calibrated at elongations ≳ \gtrsim 80 ∘ , we use it as a phenomenological reference, as in TA26.

sections.heading: IV.6.2 Distribution along the Ecliptic
sections.text: Along the ecliptic, the standard model reproduces both the gradient and the absolute surface brightness of the F-corona (Figure 7 (a)). The model indices ( − 2.31 -2.31 and − 2.33 -2.33 toward the west and east) agree with the mean of the observed eastern and western indices, and the predicted surface brightness agrees with the observations within 6%. The observations therefore support α ≃ 1.3 \alpha\simeq 1.3 at the heliocentric distances of ∼ \sim 0.2–0.35 au that dominate the F-corona at these elongations, as concluded in TA26. This value agrees with those from zodiacal light observations inside the Earth’s orbit, α = 1.3 ± 0.05 \alpha=1.3\pm 0.05 at 0.3–1 au with Helios [ 31 ] and 1.30 ± 0.08 1.30\pm 0.08 at 0.76–1.06 au with Hayabusa2# [ 51 ] , and from STEREO/HI-1A ( 1.31 1.31 –1.35; Stenborg et al. 44 ); a single power law with α ≃ 1.3 \alpha\simeq 1.3 thus describes the radial distribution of the dust from ∼ \sim 1 au down to ∼ \sim 0.2 au. The model is, however, nearly symmetric between east and west and does not reproduce the shallower eastern profiles.

Nevertheless, the F-corona constrains the vertical structure of the dust cloud at ∼ \sim 0.2–0.35 au, a region not probed by the infrared observations on which the standard model is based.

sections.heading: IV.7 Limitations
sections.text: The results of this section are subject to the following limitations. First, the zero point relies on the interpretation of the dark-side signal as foreground light uniform across the field of view (Section III.5 ); an alternative interpretation would change the indices within 15 ∘ 15^{\circ} by ≲ \lesssim 0.2 except toward the south, whereas the profiles beyond ∼ \sim 20 ∘ depend on it strongly. Second, the flat field is derived in situ from stars and is uncertain by up to ∼ \sim 0.1 mag at the edge of the field, which may contribute to the east–west asymmetry and the eastern color dependence. Third, the observation provides a single epoch and viewing geometry, so that asymmetries due to the observer position cannot be separated from intrinsic ones. Finally, the constraints on the dust distribution are derived within the ZodiSURF framework, with its scattering phase function and functional forms, and are therefore model dependent.

sections.heading: V.1 From RAW to JPEG
sections.text: To verify the results obtained in TA26, we compared the JPEG and RAW images pixel by pixel, after mapping the pixel grids onto each other.

sections.heading: V.1.1 Geometric Correction
sections.text: The radial distortion model recorded in the XMP metadata (Section II.3 ) reproduces, without any free parameter, the mapping between the JPEG and RAW pixel grids derived from 1710 stars with an rms residual of 0.40 pixels, the same as that of a free fifth-order polynomial mapping (0.39 pixels; Appendix A ). The geometric processing of the JPEG image is thus fully documented in its metadata.

The metadata of the JPEG image indicate that a vignetting correction was applied, and TA26 therefore applied no further correction. However, the vignetting model of the lens profile predicts a light falloff of only 6% at the image corners, compared with the actual ∼ \sim 70% for diffuse light (Section III.4 ). Two tests confirm that the JPEG image retains essentially the full vignetting. First, if the vignetting had been corrected in the rendering, the JPEG signal would be a function of F / T ⁡ ( ρ ) F/T(\rho) rather than of the RAW signal F F , so that pixels with the same F F would have different S S depending on ρ \rho . Instead, the smoothed JPEG signal is a tight function of F F without any radial correction (rms scatter of 1.5 DN in the green channel), whereas assuming a full correction increases the scatter to 5.0 DN. Second, photometry of the BSC5 stars in the JPEG image, linearized with the tone response derived below, shows a light loss of 0.5–0.7 mag at ρ = 0.75 \rho=0.75 , comparable to that in the RAW data. The assumption of TA26 that the vignetting had been removed by the processing is therefore not valid.

sections.heading: V.1.3 Tone Response
sections.text: The relation between the JPEG signal S S and the linear RAW signal F F is tight and monotonic but is not a single power law (Figure 11 ). Its local slope d ​ ln ⁡ S / d ​ ln ⁡ F d\ln S/d\ln F , which corresponds to Γ \Gamma in TA26, decreases from ∼ \sim 1.1–1.2 at S ≃ 15 S\simeq 15 –30 DN to ∼ \sim 0.7 at S ≃ 100 S\simeq 100 DN and ∼ \sim 0.5 at S ≃ 160 S\simeq 160 DN, nearly identically in the three channels, and neither a single power law nor the sRGB transfer function (approximately S ∝ F 1 / 2.2 S\propto F^{1/2.2} ) reproduces it. The values of Γ \Gamma derived in TA26 from stars correspond to the local slopes at S ≃ 60 S\simeq 60 –100 DN, typical of the backgrounds of the bright calibration stars, and overestimate the compression at the fainter levels of the outer profiles; their differences among the channels are not present in the actual tone response. In addition, the JPEG signal does not decrease below ∼ \sim 2–4 DN, and the JPEG channels are related to the RAW channels through a color-space transformation that mixes them.

sections.heading: VI Capabilities and Limitations of JPEG-based Analysis
sections.text: Although our results are specific to one image and one processing chain, the underlying causes are generic. We summarize them here for analyses of JPEG images from crewed missions, citizen-science programs, and archives, for which RAW data may not be available. sections.heading: VI.1 Robust and Biased Quantities
sections.text: Table 7 summarizes which quantities can be derived reliably from consumer-camera JPEG images, together with their main limitations and the remedies used in this work. Quantities that depend only on the ordering of the signal are in principle not affected by a monotonic tone response. The shapes of the isophotes are the prime example, and their robustness is verified here ( f W f_{\rm W} is the same at all steps of Table 5 ); in general, however, quantization, compression, channel mixing, and resampling may still affect them, in particular at faint levels. Other examples are tests that only require knowing which of two signals is brighter, such as the test of Section III.5 : that the darkest sky is fainter than the dark side of the Moon, which shows that the dark-side signal is not uniform on the detector, follows directly from the JPEG image (1.5–3.0 DN, compared with 2.4–7.5 DN) without any knowledge of the tone response. Geometric quantities are also robust, provided that a distortion model of sufficiently high order is used, and the geometric correction of the JPEG rendering was fully documented in the metadata. In contrast, quantities that compare signals at different levels or at different positions on the detector are biased. In our case, the tone response had the largest effect, dominating the errors of the northern and southern gradients, followed by the vignetting and pixel solid angle, which dominated the errors toward the east, and the zero point, which mattered mainly toward the south (Section V.2 ). Field stars, the natural calibrators of a JPEG image, require care: a star on a bright background measures the local slope of the tone response at the level of that background, so that a single Γ \Gamma derived from stars is an average weighted toward the bright backgrounds of the calibration stars; the radial decrease of the background and the vignetting are partly degenerate when the Sun is near the field center.

We fitted this relation to the BSC5 stars in the JPEG image ( ∼ \sim 200 per channel, with S B ≃ 2 S_{B}\simeq 2 –130 DN), representing log 10 ⁡ ( d ​ S / d ​ F ) \log_{10}(dS/dF) as a cubic polynomial in log 10 ⁡ S B \log_{10}S_{B} , and integrated it to obtain the tone response up to an additive constant. The reconstructed tone response agrees with that derived from the RAW data within ∼ \sim 10% over S = 15 S=15 –150 DN, and the derived vignetting agrees within 0.06–0.18 mag at ρ = 0.75 \rho=0.75 (Figure 13 ). Using this calibration with the pixel solid angle and the zero point in surface brightness, and setting the linear signal to zero at the black level of the JPEG image, reproduces the eastern and western indices of the RAW data within 0.2 and the north–south to east–west brightness ratio within 0.05, compared with errors of up to ∼ \sim 3 and 0.07 for the method of TA26. The northern and southern indices still differ by 0.04–1.0, mainly because the additive constant of the tone response cannot be determined from the stars: with its true value, the residuals decrease to ≲ \lesssim 0.06 in the red channel and 0.3–0.7 in the green and blue channels, the remainder reflecting the partial degeneracy between the tone response and the vignetting. The method is demonstrated here for one image; it requires stars on backgrounds spanning a wide range of brightness (here 2–130 DN) and constrains the tone response only over that range; it is applicable to images with large variations of diffuse brightness, such as the F-corona and the zodiacal light, bright nebulae, the Milky Way, or skies with strong gradients in twilight or moonlight, but not to images with a uniformly dark background.

sections.heading: VI.3 Recommendations
sections.text: We recommend the following for analyses of consumer-camera JPEG images of diffuse emission when RAW data are not available. 1. Inspect the metadata for the rendering software, lens profile, and recorded corrections, and do not assume that a flagged correction is complete. 2. Derive the astrometric solution with a distortion model of sufficiently high order (e.g., by increasing the SIP order of Astrometry.net from its default value), and compute the pixel solid angle from it and the recorded distortion model (Appendix A ). 3. Calibrate the tone response as a function of signal level rather than with a single Γ \Gamma , e.g., with the method of Section VI.2 , and restrict quantitative analyses to the range of levels covered by the calibration. 4. Measure the vignetting with field stars, and correct the diffuse emission for both the vignetting and the pixel solid angle. 5. Test whether the zero-point reference (e.g., an occulter) contains light that is not present over the rest of the field, by comparing it with the darkest parts of the sky. 6. Prefer quantities that are invariant under monotonic transformations, such as isophote shapes, for the main conclusions, and treat radial gradients at faint levels, color differences, and comparisons across the field with caution.

sections.heading: VII Summary
sections.text: We reanalyzed the Artemis II total solar eclipse images analyzed in TA26, using the RAW sensor data of the camera. The main results are as follows. 1. The RAW data were calibrated in situ with field stars. The vignetting of the lens at full aperture, combined with the variation of the pixel solid angle, reduces the signal of diffuse light by ∼ \sim 70% at the outer edge of the calibrated field. The signal on the dark side of the Moon is light rather than an instrumental offset, and is most naturally explained as foreground light that is uniform across the field of view; it was subtracted in surface brightness. 2. Between 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} and 15 ∘ 15^{\circ} elongation, the radial profiles of the F-corona follow power laws with indices of − 2.04 -2.04 to − 2.33 -2.33 (east), − 2.48 -2.48 to − 2.51 -2.51 (west), − 2.43 -2.43 to − 2.74 -2.74 (north), and − 2.51 -2.51 to − 2.68 -2.68 (south), consistent with previous space-based observations. The isophotes with semimajor axes of ∼ \sim 17 ∘ –22 ∘ have flattening indices of ∼ \sim 0.6–0.7 and superellipse indices of ∼ \sim 1.5–1.6. The absolute surface brightness along the ecliptic is ∼ \sim 26 MJy sr -1 ( ± 7 % \pm 7\% ) at 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} . 3. Within the framework of the ZodiSURF model, the observations support a radial density index of α ≃ 1.3 \alpha\simeq 1.3 down to heliocentric distances of ∼ \sim 0.2 au, and indicate a vertical distribution of the dust that is much less concentrated toward the symmetry plane than in the standard model; a model in which the vertical concentration parameter decreases toward the Sun as η ∝ r 0.4 ​ – ​ 0.6 \eta\propto r^{0.4\text{--}0.6} reproduces all the measured observables, although its gradient depends on the zero point. 4. The JPEG image analyzed in TA26 retains essentially the full vignetting of the lens, and its tone response is not a single power law. These two effects, together with the treatment of the zero point, account for the steep radial profiles, the north–south asymmetry of the indices, and the color dependence reported in TA26. 5. JPEG-based analyses can nevertheless recover robust physical results: the flattened morphology, the negligible contribution of the K-corona, and α ≃ 1.3 \alpha\simeq 1.3 derived in TA26 survive the RAW analysis, and isophote shapes are robust in JPEG images. Radial gradients, comparisons across the field, and colors, however, require calibration of the vignetting and of the tone response (Table 7 ); the tone response can be reconstructed from field stars when the image contains a wide range of diffuse brightness. These results also bear on future observations of the F-corona from lunar orbit [ 16 , 12 ] : foreground light within the instrument field must be characterized, e.g., by observing with the Moon at different detector positions; a laboratory flat field would improve on the in situ calibration; and linear data are essential. With RAW data, even a handheld consumer camera operated by a crew member yields F-corona measurements comparable to those of dedicated space-based imagers. Its brightness distribution traces the structure of the inner zodiacal cloud. Because the F-corona must be observed against the photospheric glare, observations have relied on coronagraphs and heliospheric imagers, such as LASCO on board SOHO [ 28 ] , the Heliospheric Imager on board STEREO [ 44 ] , and WISPR on board the Parker Solar Probe [ 43 ] , or on eclipse-like geometries in which a planetary body blocks the solar disk [ 17 ] . The use of the lunar disk as a natural, low-stray-light occulter dates back to the Surveyor missions [ 36 , 7 ] and has been revisited as a concept for routine coronal observations from lunar orbit [ 16 , 12 ] . The Artemis II crewed lunar flyby provided such a geometry. On 2026 April 7, about two hours after closest approach, the crew photographed the totally eclipsed Sun from the Orion spacecraft with a handheld consumer digital camera, and NASA released the image art002e009301 as an 8-bit RGB JPEG image on the same day. Using this image, Tsumura and Arimatsu [50, hereafter TA26] investigated the large-scale morphology of the optical F-corona over solar elongations of ∼ \sim 7 ∘ –38 ∘ . They reported a flattened distribution aligned with the ecliptic (flattening indices f = 0.52 f=0.52 – 0.56 0.56 ; Equation 5 in Section IV.3 ), radial profiles that are systematically steeper than those derived from STEREO/HI-1A [ 44 ] , and a radial dust density index of α ∼ 1.3 \alpha\sim 1.3 from a comparison with the ZodiSURF model [ 38 ] . I.2 Consumer-camera JPEG images as astronomical data Images taken with consumer digital cameras are increasingly used for scientific purposes, including measurements of night-sky brightness and artificial light at night [ 18 , 41 ] , photometry of bright stars [ 11 ] , and morphological studies in which absolute calibration is not required [ 34 , 27 ] . Rendered products such as JPEG images are often the only form in which an observation is made public, especially for opportunistic observations from crewed spacecraft. A JPEG image, however, is a rendering of the incident flux rather than a measurement of it: the processing chain typically includes demosaicing, white balancing, a color-space transformation that mixes the camera channels, a tone curve, optional lens corrections, quantization to 8 bits, and lossy compression, most of which are camera- and software-specific and poorly documented [ 9 , e.g.,] . Any analysis of a JPEG image must therefore assume a model for the inverse of this chain, which usually cannot be verified from the JPEG image itself. TA26 defined the zero point of each channel by the signal on the dark side of the lunar disk, modeled the tone response as a single power law, S ∝ F Γ S\propto F^{\Gamma} , between the JPEG signal S S and the incident flux F F , with Γ = 0.700 \Gamma=0.700 , 0.725, and 0.825 for the red, green, and blue channels calibrated with field stars, and assumed that vignetting had been removed by the processing, as indicated by the image metadata. Each of these steps was reasonable given the available data, but none of them could be tested independently. I.3 This work: RAW data as ground truth On 2026 October 7, the original camera RAW files of the Artemis II lunar flyby images were archived in the NASA Planetary Data System [ 4 ] . For art002e009301 , this provides the 14-bit sensor data of exactly the same exposure that was analyzed in TA26. Such a pairing of a rendered JPEG image and the corresponding RAW data for a scientifically analyzed astronomical target offers a rare opportunity to check every assumption of a JPEG-based analysis quantitatively. The purpose of this paper is twofold. First, we re-derive the properties of the F-corona from the RAW data with a full reduction, including an in situ flat-field correction, a characterization of the zero point, and an absolute calibration. A second frame with a three times longer exposure ( art002e009300 ), reduced independently, provides a key check that the results do not depend on a single image. Second, we use the RAW data to evaluate how each step of the JPEG-based analysis affected the results of TA26, and we assess which quantities can and cannot be derived reliably from consumer-camera JPEG images. Throughout this paper, “ground truth” refers to the closest available representation of the sensor measurements: the RAW data are themselves stored with a non-reversible compression (Section II.2 ) and are therefore not strictly identical to the original sensor output. Section II describes the data, Section III the reduction of the RAW data, and Section IV the properties of the F-corona derived from them. Section V compares the RAW and JPEG analyses, Section VI discusses the capabilities and limitations of JPEG-based analysis, and Section VII summarizes this work. II.2 RAW data We used the original camera files in Nikon Electronic Format (NEF) from the Artemis II Crew Camera Bundle of the NASA Planetary Data System [ 4 ] , rather than the processed products of the bundle [ 5 ] , so that the entire reduction could be controlled. The NEF files are recorded with the “High efficiency ⋆ \star ” (HE ∗ ) option of the camera, a non-reversible compression based on the TicoRAW codec [ 24 ] , which, according to the manufacturer, produces pictures that compare favorably in quality to those recorded with lossless compression [ 35 ] . We converted the NEF files into the Digital Negative (DNG) format with Adobe DNG Converter [ 2 , version 18.7;] , which decodes the HE ∗ data without further processing, and read the DNG files with rawpy [ 40 ] . The conversion preserves the undemosaiced sensor data; possible effects of the HE ∗ compression on faint signals could not be evaluated directly, but the linear response of the stellar signals (Section III.6 ) and the agreement of all results between the two frames, whose signal levels differ by a factor of three, show no evidence of them. We use the full sensor area (Table 1 ); the default crop of the DNG files starts at pixel ( x , y ) = ( 12 , 8 ) (x,y)=(12,8) and matches the size of the released JPEG image. II.3 JPEG image For the comparison with TA26, we used the JPEG version of art002e009301 released by NASA. According to its metadata, it was rendered from the RAW file with Adobe Photoshop Lightroom Classic about four hours after the exposure, using the Adobe lens profile for the lens and camera with both distortion and vignetting corrections flagged as applied. The coefficients of the radial distortion model are recorded, and the full lens profile, including a vignetting model, is also embedded in the DNG files. The parameters of the other rendering steps (tone curve, color rendering, and any local adjustments) are not recorded. The actual processing is evaluated in Section V.1 . Systematic effects fixed to the detector, such as a non-radial component of the vignetting that differs between the channels, would however affect both frames in the same way, and we regard this color dependence as tentative. It cannot be explained by contamination from the K-corona: the K-corona has the color of the solar spectrum, whereas the zodiacal light is redder than the solar spectrum from optical to near-infrared wavelengths [ 32 , 49 , e.g.,] , and the K-corona decreases more steeply with elongation than the F-corona [ 53 , 20 ] ; its contamination would thus steepen the profiles in the blue channel rather than flatten them. As a further test, TA26 compared the profiles along two coronal streamers seen in a publicly available LASCO C3 [ 8 ] image taken 12 minutes before art002e009301 with those along the opposite directions. We repeated this comparison with the same LASCO C3 image and the same sectors as TA26 (Figure 6 ). The ratio of the “on” to “off” profiles is close to unity at the smallest elongations and departs from it outward, decreasing to 0.45–0.75 for S1 and increasing to 1.2–1.9 for S2 at ∼ \sim 20 ∘ , consistently in the two frames. A K-coronal contribution would instead produce an excess along the streamers that is largest near the Sun. The departures follow the large-scale asymmetries found above: the S2 sectors coincide with the eastern and western profiles, and the S1 “off” sector lies in the northeastern quadrant, toward which the isophotes are displaced. We therefore find no evidence for a K-coronal contribution, in agreement with TA26, but unlike TA26, we find a dimming along the streamer only for S1 (see Section V.2 ).
